en: {The Gazing at the Moon}
Hariḥ Oṃ.
Maheśvara said: With the internal object of focus and the gaze directed externally, free from blinking and opening— the this is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, hidden among all [teachings].
When the yogi remains with his mind and breath dissolved within the internal object of focus,
looking outward with a perfectly steady gaze, he should always remain thus;
this indeed is the Khecarī Mudrā, which comes about through the grace of the Guru.
If that reality which is free from both the void and the non-void vibrates, it is the state of Śambhu.
With eyes half-closed, mind steady, and the gaze fixed for a moment on the tip of the nose,
even the sun and moon have attained dissolution; his body has become motionless,
and he shines intensely as the supreme light-form, devoid of all external things.
That which is the supreme reality attains that state; what more need be said?
When the dissolution within the womb is realized in that state,
that dissolution itself should be understood as being conjoined with a satisfied Guru.
Behold that consciousness within the body, the witness of the arising and passing away of all beings, which is the nectar of the mass of full bliss.
If the mind is elsewhere, the power is elsewhere, and the vital breath is elsewhere,
O lady of beautiful hips, one does not attain success even in hundreds of millions of eons.
O Goddess, from where can knowledge arise as long as the mind lives?
As long as the mind does not die, even though the vital breath (prāṇa) continues to live;
when both this prāṇa and the mind reach dissolution, [then knowledge arises].
That man attains liberation; no other does so in any way whatsoever.
He who constantly maintains his attention without distraction upon the subtle seeds of pleasure and so forth within the conjunctions and disjunctions of the signs [of perception] is truly vigilant.
Wherever there is sight, there is the mind, along with the eternal elements and senses;
that is the power of the elements, for sight has reached dissolution into its objective.
Where there is steadiness of vision and mind, there indeed is the vital breath (māruta);
this may be some such state, which is esteemed by the perfected ones (siddhas) as being without spokes.
The form situated at the tip of the eye, existing both externally and internally, is seen even at the tip of the eye;
yet by the eye alone, one does not see it.
Standing eternally at the tip of the eye, like a gem shimmering in the sky—
by seeing that all-pervading Śambhu, one is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
The light of the self, the light of the mind, and the light of the eye do not perceive it;
that light which is both external and internal—that light is called Śiva.
As long as the moving wind does not enter the central path,
as long as the vital breath has not awakened and the bindu has not become firm,
and as long as that which is similar to the void does not arise as the essence, there is no state of Unmanā.
If one speaks all of that, it is merely deceptive and false prattle.
One who is devoted to constant practice, faithful to the guru, and steadfast,
yet does not know the innate nature, proceeds like a blind man.
The new moon, the first day of the lunar fortnight, and the full moon are concealed;
poison, at will, is rendered stainless and is served everywhere.
At the outset, filled with affection, they protect [the people], yet they wander through the worlds;
deceived by false hypocrisy, they do not know things as they truly are.
The new moon, the first day of the lunar fortnight, and the full moon are concealed;
indeed, the stainless poison resides within everyone.
Matsyendra said:
"O Śaṅkara, how is that designation 'Amāvāsyā', 'Pratipad', and 'Paurṇamāsī' explained? Please explain everything according to its true nature."
Īśvara said:
The first lunar day (pratipad) is the opening of the eyes; the new moon (amāvāsyā) is the closing of the eyes;
that which lasts until half-observation is called the full moon (parṇamāsī).
What is expressed by the word "Kāma," and what is expressed by "Poison"?
Who possesses the nature of the stainless? Explain this according to reality.
The Lord devours time at every step, and likewise on my new moon day;
having made the path firm, it becomes so and not otherwise.
Through desire arises the longing for sense objects, and from that desire comes absorption in them; one should constantly abandon both of these and take refuge in the stainless.
Another person should renounce everything if he desires his own welfare.
And there is death in another way because of having experienced [the fruits of karma].
Having placed the mind within the power [of consciousness], and having the mind moving within that power,
one should perceive the mind with the mind and meditate upon that supreme state.
Matsyendra and Bīja—how are they designated, and what is the characteristic of the Bindu?
How does the Bindu arise? Explain this according to the true nature of reality.
The Lord is indeed the mind alone, for it is the seed and the cause of both origination and maintenance;
from the mind the *bindu* is produced, just as milk [yields] that which has the nature of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Matsyendra[-nātha] is the crest[-lock] that pervades everything from the peak of the mountain to the limits of pleasure and pain;
it flows through the aperture of the uvula— what kind of bond could there be for it?
The Lord is neither situated in the midst of bondage nor possessed of a single causal mind;
where the power (*śakti*) is in the center of the moon, there is bondage.
Having known the true division of the Suṣumnā, one should release [the breath] through the left while keeping it moving toward the center.
Having performed this in the place of the moon, one should restrain it within the nostril;
this is declared to be Matsyendra, the breath-drop (*vāsubindu*), as well as the reality (*tattva*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
"I do not know the six cakras; please be gracious and tell me.
The Lord said: "The Ādhāra, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and Maṇipūra as the third."
The unstruck (*anāhata*) and the pure (*viśuddha*), and the sixth is the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*);
then the hub is said to be the anus, and the self-sustained (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the generative organ.
Maṇipūra is in the region of the navel; Anāhata resides in the heart; Viśuddha is in the region of the throat; and the Ājñā-cakra is at the crown of the head.
Having fully understood the six cakras, one should enter the fixed mandala;
having drawn in the wind, one should enter it and likewise direct it upward.
One should practice in this manner until one becomes identical with the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
one should practice while joining the wind, the bindu, and the cakra within the mind, again and again.
Through a single concentration, yogis attain immortality simultaneously;
just as fire residing within wood does not arise without friction.
In the same way, through the yoga of practice, the light of knowledge does not indeed shine outwardly,
just as a lamp inside a jar does not illuminate the exterior.
When [the seed] has reached maturity, it shines like the flame of a lamp;
its own nature is said to be the "pot," for that very word refers to the lamp itself.
Through the words of the Guru, the knowledge of Brahman becomes manifest.
Having obtained a teacher as their helmsman and having refined the subtle internal channels,
those who are intent on the practice of the vehicle cross the ocean of existence.
Matsyendra said:
"By the grace of your feet, I am liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
You are my refuge, O God, Lord of Gods; it is not otherwise for me, O Śaṅkara."
Having heard these words of the Lord of the Immortals, the Blessed Śiva entered [the body];
he said, "Go, my son, upon the earth; you shall uplift the three worlds."
[Thus ends the Candrāvalokana composed by Maheśvara.]
Salutations to the illustrious Lord Guru.
